title: Age Bracket
story: A government portal once issued a driving license to a -3-year-old 'person' because no one validated the age input. Multi-invariant types prevent these absurd states from ever existing.
why: Multiple invariants on a single type encode complex real-world constraints that no function can ever violate.
analogy: Multiple invariants are like airport security layers — ID check, baggage scan, metal detector. Each catches different threats, together they catch everything.
try_it: Add `can_retire` (>= 65) and `can_drink` (>= 21). Then create an array of Ages from 0 to 100 and print which ones can drive vs. vote — watch how the invariants protect every single value.
tips: Each invariant should test ONE rule — don't combine unrelated checks into a single line
Boolean query methods on invariant types NEVER need defensive checks — the invariant already proved validity
Consider capping at the high end too — a 500-year-old 'person' is a data entry bug
common_mistakes: Hardcoding constants like 16 and 18 inside invariants when they should be threshold query methods
Forgetting that `next_birthday` must handle the cap — incrementing from 150 would violate the invariant
Creating an Age with `-1` and expecting the compiler to warn — invariants are checked at runtime (or by Z3), not by the type checker
